newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Nemtsov faces huge task as new Russian energy head.
newsitem.headline: Nemtsov faces huge task as new Russian energy head.

text.p: Russia's vital oil and gas sector is unlikely to change radically any time soon despite Thursday's appointment of dynamic First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov as fuel and energy minister, Western energy executives and analysts said.

His clout may raise the sector's profile in the political arena, they said. But not even the "golden boy" of President Boris Yeltsin's new reformist cabinet could provide quick answers in a sector starved of investment and bogged down in bureaucracy.
"It (his appointment) won't be as heavy hitting," said Peter Houlder, managing director of CentreInvest Group consultancy.

A big problem for Nemtsov will be finding time for his new duties in a crammed schedule, analysts said. He is already in charge of restructuring Russia's huge enterprises which enjoy de facto monopolies.
"It's hard to see how he won't be distracted by his cabinet duties -- he's got an awful lot on his plate," Houlder said.
Another major question mark hanging over Nemtsov is his lack of experience in the oil and gas sector, which is traditionally ruled from behind the scenes by powerful oil barons.
"He is very inexperienced in this sphere," said one executive. "But at least he should bring a breath of fresh air to the business."
An analyst said the choice of his deputies in the ministry could therefore be as important as his nomination itself. "The identity of his deputies will of course be of vital importance," he said.
Moscow-based Western oil and gas executives said the list of pressing issues facing the ministry was daunting, and Nemtsov could make a difference only in the long term.
Russia's main concern was to prevent a repeat of the steep fall in output it suffered during the early 1990s, they said.

Some analysts said this could be achieved only by passing a list of Russian oil and gas reserves qualifying for development with Western partners under controversial production sharing agreements. This process is currently stalled.

"The production sharing agreements are the crux of the issue," said Jeremy Hudson, oil and gas analyst at Salomon Brothers in London. "The lack of investment would manifest itself in an output decline."
Others stressed the need for reforms to tax and transport costs, a major reason why they are not able to invest in output to stabilise recent steep falls in output declines.
Crude oil output from Russia, the world's third largest producer but once its biggest, fell two percent last year to 293 million tonnes (5.9 million barrels per day).

The rate of decline between 1995 and 1996 was well down on the 1994-1995 period. But analysts said this phenomenon was only temporary, and that sharper production declines could resume by the end of the century unless big investments were made.
Nemtsov also faces the monumental task of reforming Russia's sprawling pipeline system, still controlled by state-owned pipeline monopoly Transneft.
Companies have criticised a lack of transparency in the process of allocating access to the crowded system as well as high domestic and export tariffs.

Nemtsov may succeed in forcing tariffs down, but in the long run what Russia needs is fresh finance for new oil and oil product export routes, boosting the amount of hard currency its producers can earn, analysts said.
"At the moment all he could achieve would be to shuffle the pack. The pack will not actually get any bigger," said one analyst.

Russia exported 105 million tonnes (2.1 million bpd) of oil in 1996 outside the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), a nine percent jump from 1995. But analysts said the room for further increases was strictly limited.
While Nemtsov's policies on oil remain a mystery, those on gas are clearer. He has already boosted government influence over gas monopoly Gazprom, the world's largest producer.

But he stopped short of demanding the company be broken up, a move strongly opposed by conservative factions in the lower house of parliament, the State Duma. Russian natural gas output hit 601 billion cubic metres in 1996, 128 billion of which was exported outside the CIS.
